newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid agencies to test Zaire rebel promise of access.
newsitem.headline: Aid agencies to test Zaire rebel promise of access.

text.p: Aid agencies intend to test a rebel promise of access to thousands of Rwandan refugees hiding in Zaire's forests by returning on Tuesday to a checkpoint where they were blocked.

The rebels failed the first test on Monday of rebel leader Laurent Kabila's promise on Sunday of free access when an aid convoy was turned back from a military checkpoint at Biaro, 41 km (25 miles) south of the northeastern capital of Kisangani.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said it hoped to fly out to Rwanda on Tuesday from Kisangani 250 refugees collected from the remnants of Biaro camp and some of 1,000 others who had reached the city.

Before they were turned back on Monday, aid workers and journalists saw some 5,000 Hutu refugees emerge from the forests and return to Biaro, which they said they fled last week after being attacked by villagers and the Tutsi-dominated rebels.
The bad condition of the refugees shocked even aid officials hardened by years of dealing with the Rwandan refugee crisis.
Dozens of those emerging from the forest were desperately ill -- many with cholera, doctors said -- and others bore horrific wounds from the attacks that sparked their exodus.

Rebel authorities have denied attacking camps at Kasese and Biaro last week. They said rebels intervened and were ambushed by Rwandan militiamen among the refugees only after villagers attacked the camps in retaliation for the killing of six Zairean civilians by refugees.
But in Biaro on Monday, almost nothing appeared to have been looted. Foodstocks had instead been destroyed in a way one aid official described as "a deliberate starvation policy".
A bid by rebels to portray themselves as caring for refugees was dismissed by another aid official as "a cynical charade".
Two rebels, immaculately clad in fresh uniforms, emerged from the camp wearing surgical gloves and saying they had spent five days helping the refugees.
But in the more than one hour aid officials and journalists spent at the camp, one rebel spent most of his time shooing away any refugee who approached him.
The Hutu refugees appeared terrified. One priority for aid workers was to bury the dozens of bodies in the camps.
More than 30 were seen on Monday. Some, aid officials said, had died of illness while others had been brutally attacked.
The stench of decaying corpses blew in from deeper within the jungle and refugees emerging from the forest reported seeing hundreds of bodies there.
The 85,000 Hutu refugees from Kasese and Biaro were among up to 100,000 south of Kisangani missing since aid agencies and journalists were barred from the camps by rebels last week.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
An outbreak of cholera was cited by rebels as the reason for delaying the start of a planned U.N. airlift of the refugees.

Kabila demanded on Sunday that aid agencies repatriate all the remaining Rwandan refugees in Zaire within 60 days. The United States, UNHCR and U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan say the deadline is unrealistic.
Aid workers say it is impossible to repatriate all 100,000 south of Kisangani and another 250,000 Rwandan refugees who are still unaccounted for in Zaire even with full rebel cooperation.

One aid official described as "preposterous" a demand by rebels for an $8 departure tax for each refugee evacuated. Other aid officials said they believed that Rwanda was also insisting on the same amount for each Hutu refugee as a landing tax.
Aid officials said they were also told that rebel authorities had raised a landing tax on planes at Kisangani from $250 to $4,000.
